I am a geomatics and remote sensing specialist with advanced Master-level training, based in Cape Town, South Africa. I use geospatial data and deep learning to address environmental and territorial challenges, from vegetation mapping to environmental health assessment.

My background spans the University of Antananarivo (Master 2 in Earth Physics, thesis defended in August 2026), the University of La Réunion (international credit mobility in Geomatics and Remote Sensing), and research internships at INERIS in France and the Institute and Observatory of Geophysics of Antananarivo (IOGA) in Madagascar. I am currently pursuing an MSc in Applied Mathematics at Stellenbosch University to strengthen my quantitative and analytical skills.

My recent work has focused on two main areas:

  • Remote sensing and deep learning: automatic detection of individual vegetable, allotment and ornamental gardens from 20 cm aerial imagery (IGN BD ORTHO). A U-Net with a ResNet-34 encoder reached 83 % overall accuracy versus 58 % for Random Forest, and an IoU of 82 % on allotment gardens in the Oise test area.
  • GIS and environmental data: structuring a PostgreSQL / PostGIS road network database and automating the collection and harmonization of open road traffic data (94 of 101 departments inventoried, 291,460 road segments) for environmental health risk assessment.

Earlier, at IOGA, I produced Sentinel-2 land cover maps of Ankarafantsika National Park (2018 and 2023, with overall accuracies of 91.4 % and 93.0 %) and built an ecosystem accounting approach in SAGA GIS.

I am particularly interested in scientific and applied projects combining satellite Earth observation, spatial modeling and vegetation dynamics, especially forest disturbance and recovery monitoring, with a focus on international opportunities in Europe and South Africa.

docs.title: Suivi en temps réel des bus Car Jaune avec PostGIS¶
Aperçu¶
docs.text:
Ce notebook récupère la position des bus Car Jaune via le flux GTFS-RT, identifie pour chaque véhicule l'arrêt le plus proche grâce au GTFS statique, affiche le tout sur une carte interactive, puis enregistre l'état du réseau dans une table PostGIS.

Zone d'étude : La Réunion (réseau Car Jaune) Statut : Terminé

docs.title: Méthodes et outils¶
docs.text:
Sources de données

  • Flux GTFS-RT Car Jaune (positions des véhicules en temps réel) : https://pysae.com/api/v2/groups/car-jaune/gtfs-rt
  • GTFS statique Car Jaune (fichier stops.txt, arrêts du réseau) : https://pysae.com/api/v2/groups/car-jaune/gtfs/pub

Étapes de traitement

  1. Télécharger le flux GTFS-RT et l'archive GTFS statique
  2. Charger les arrêts (stops.txt) dans un GeoDataFrame
  3. Calculer pour chaque bus l'arrêt le plus proche (distance en mètres, projection UTM 40S)
  4. Cartographier les bus et les arrêts avec Folium
  5. Créer la table PostGIS et y enregistrer les positions

Outils utilisés

Outil Rôle requests Téléchargement du flux GTFS-RT et du GTFS statique gtfs-realtime-bindings Décodage du flux GTFS-RT (protobuf) pandas / geopandas Lecture des arrêts, géodonnées, reprojection shapely Géométries ponctuelles des bus folium Carte web interactive SQLAlchemy + psycopg2 Connexion et écriture dans PostgreSQL PostgreSQL / PostGIS Stockage des positions (geometry(Point, 4326))

docs.title: Configuration¶
docs.text: Import des bibliothèques.

docs.title: Données¶
docs.text: Téléchargement du flux temps réel (positions des bus) et du GTFS statique (arrêts), puis chargement des arrêts dans un GeoDataFrame en WGS84 (EPSG:4326).

docs.title: Arrêt le plus proche de chaque bus¶
docs.text: Pour chaque véhicule, les arrêts et le bus sont reprojetés en UTM zone 40S (EPSG:32740) afin de calculer des distances en mètres, puis l'arrêt à distance minimale est retenu. Les marqueurs des bus sont ajoutés à leur couche Folium au passage.

docs.title: Distribution spatiale¶
docs.text: Carte interactive centrée sur La Réunion avec deux couches activables : les bus (une couleur par véhicule) et les arrêts du réseau.

docs.title: Enregistrement dans PostGIS¶
docs.text:
Les positions sont stockées dans la table public.carjaune_vehicles_rt :

Colonne Type Description vehicle_id text (clé primaire) Identifiant du véhicule timestamp bigint Horodatage Unix du relevé geom geometry(Point, 4326) Position du bus nearest_stop text Nom de l'arrêt le plus proche

À chaque exécution, la table est vidée puis remplie avec les positions les plus récentes.

docs.title: Résultats clés¶
docs.text:
• Relevé du 22/11/2025 vers 21h55 : 3 véhicules actifs dans le flux GTFS-RT, à comparer aux 458 arrêts du GTFS statique.
  • Chaque bus est rattaché à son arrêt le plus proche : La Veuve (environ 1 020 m), Gare St-Louis (environ 625 m) et RDT Etang-Salé (environ 43 m).
  • Les distances sont à vol d'oiseau (projection UTM 40S), pas le long du trajet : un arrêt proche peut être de l'autre côté d'un relief ou sur une autre ligne.
  • La table est vidée avant chaque insertion, elle ne contient donc que le dernier état du réseau. Pour conserver l'historique des passages, il faudrait supprimer le DELETE et utiliser une clé (vehicle_id, timestamp).

docs.title: Real-Time Car Jaune Bus Tracking with PostGIS¶
Overview¶
docs.text:
This notebook retrieves Car Jaune bus positions from the GTFS-RT feed, finds the nearest stop for each vehicle using the static GTFS, displays everything on an interactive map, and stores the current state of the network in a PostGIS table.

Study Area: La Réunion (Car Jaune network) Role: Solo project Status: Completed

docs.title: Methods & Tools¶
docs.text:
Data Sources

  • Car Jaune GTFS-RT feed (real-time vehicle positions): https://pysae.com/api/v2/groups/car-jaune/gtfs-rt
  • Car Jaune static GTFS (stops.txt, network stops): https://pysae.com/api/v2/groups/car-jaune/gtfs/pub

Processing Steps

  1. Download the GTFS-RT feed and the static GTFS archive
  2. Load the stops (stops.txt) into a GeoDataFrame
  3. Compute the nearest stop for each bus (distance in metres, UTM 40S projection)
  4. Map buses and stops with Folium
  5. Create the PostGIS table and store the positions

Tools Used

Tool Purpose requests Downloading the GTFS-RT feed and static GTFS gtfs-realtime-bindings Decoding the GTFS-RT feed (protobuf) pandas / geopandas Reading stops, spatial data, reprojection shapely Point geometries for buses folium Interactive web map SQLAlchemy + psycopg2 Connecting to and writing in PostgreSQL PostgreSQL / PostGIS Storing positions (geometry(Point, 4326))

docs.title: Setup¶
docs.text: Library imports.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: Download the real-time feed (bus positions) and the static GTFS (stops), then load the stops into a GeoDataFrame in WGS84 (EPSG:4326).

docs.title: Nearest stop for each bus¶
docs.text: For each vehicle, the stops and the bus are reprojected to UTM zone 40S (EPSG:32740) so distances are in metres, and the stop with the minimum distance is kept. Bus markers are added to their Folium layer along the way.

docs.title: Spatial Distribution¶
docs.text: Interactive map centred on La Réunion with two toggleable layers: buses (one colour per vehicle) and network stops.

docs.title: Storing in PostGIS¶
docs.text:
Positions are stored in the table public.carjaune_vehicles_rt:

Column Type Description vehicle_id text (primary key) Vehicle identifier timestamp bigint Unix timestamp of the observation geom geometry(Point, 4326) Bus position nearest_stop text Name of the nearest stop

On each run, the table is emptied and refilled with the latest positions.

docs.title: Key Findings¶
docs.text:
• Snapshot of 22/11/2025 around 21:55: 3 active vehicles in the GTFS-RT feed, against 458 stops in the static GTFS.
  • Each bus is matched to its nearest stop: La Veuve (about 1,020 m), Gare St-Louis (about 625 m) and RDT Etang-Salé (about 43 m).
  • Distances are straight-line (UTM 40S projection), not along the route: a nearby stop may sit across relief or on a different line.
  • The table is emptied before each insert, so it only holds the latest state of the network. To keep a history of passages, remove the DELETE and use a (vehicle_id, timestamp) key.

docs.title: Ecosystem Natural Capital Accounting of Land Cover, Ecosystem Infrastructure and Water Resources in Ankarafantsika National Park (2018–2023)
docs.text: Land cover of Ankarafantsika National Park (PNA) and its surroundings in 2018 and 2023, mapped from Sentinel-2 imagery with Random Forest (17 classes).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I applied the Ecosystem Natural Capital Accounting (CECN) quick-start package of the Convention on Biological Diversity (Weber, 2014) to Ankarafantsika National Park and its surroundings, and built three biophysical accounts for 2018 and 2023: a land cover account, an ecosystem infrastructure account (the capacity of ecosystems to keep providing intangible services) and a water resource account. Land cover is mapped from Sentinel-2 imagery with Random Forest, and every other account is built on top of those maps. The goal is to give park managers a measurable summary of the state and evolution of the park's natural capital.

Study Area: Ankarafantsika National Park (136,513 ha, IUCN category II) and its surroundings, Boeny region, north-west Madagascar (493,045 ha mapped) Duration: August 2024 – June 2025 (Master's thesis, Physics and Applications, Earth Physics track) Role: Solo project (hosted by the Laboratory of Environmental Geophysics and Remote Sensing, IOGA, University of Antananarivo; supervised by two professors) Partners: Madagascar National Parks, Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (as shown on the report cover) Status: Completed

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Study area: Ankarafantsika National Park and the nine communes it straddles, in the Boeny region.

Data Sources

  • Sentinel-2 Level-1C imagery, 2018 and 2023, dry and wet seasons, cloud cover below 20 % (processed in Google Earth Engine)
  • Field GPS points collected in August 2024 to build training parcels
  • Field surveys: 35 people interviewed in four fokontany along National Road 4, a socio-economic survey of 75 people, and five ecological plots
  • SRTM digital elevation model (30 m) for the watersheds; HydroSHEDS, HydroRIVERS, GloRiC, HydroLAKES and WHYMAP for rivers, lakes and groundwater
  • CHIRPS annual rainfall, WorldClim 30-year normals and WaPOR v3 evapotranspiration (300 m)
  • INSTAT household data (2018), building counts from high-resolution imagery as a household proxy for 2023, OpenStreetMap roads, Global Dam Watch dams, and park tourism statistics

Field GPS points used to delineate training parcels (August 2024).

Methodological workflow, from Sentinel-2 images and ancillary data to the three accounts.

docs.title: Part 1: Land cover account
docs.text:
1. Corrected Sentinel-2 Level-1C images for atmosphere with SIAC in Google Earth Engine, masked clouds and computed NDVI, NDWI and BSI.
  2. Estimated the percentage of tree cover for each pixel with Random Forest regression, then split it into forest classes (closed, semi-open, open) with a Bayesian Gaussian mixture, using a 30 % canopy minimum as the forest definition.
  3. Classified the other land cover classes with Random Forest, merged both outputs and cleaned the result with a 3 × 3 majority filter (17 classes in total).
  4. Validated each map with stratified random points interpreted on very-high-resolution imagery, using the area-based estimators of Olofsson et al. (2014).
  5. Built the change matrix between 2018 and 2023, removed impossible transitions (for example open water to forest) and classified every change into one of seven flow types (lf1 to lf7) to obtain opening stocks, gains, losses and closing stocks.

Land cover nomenclature, following the CECN ecosystem land cover units.

Land cover change flows used to build the account.

docs.title: Part 2: Ecosystem infrastructure account
docs.text:
1. Built the Landscape Ecosystem Potential for each watershed as the product of three indices: the Green Landscape Background Index (biomass potential × biotic regulation capacity, smoothed with a Gaussian filter in SAGA GIS), the High Natural Value Index (park zoning) and the landscape fragmentation index (effective mesh size).
  2. Built the River Ecosystem Potential from a river accessibility index (length × ln of discharge, adjusted for annual rainfall), a river natural value index and a river fragmentation index (based on the number of dams, 1 / ln(x + e)).
  3. Added both to obtain the Total Ecosystem Infrastructure Potential (TEIP), then computed access to services, a sustainable-use index (TEIP at the end of the period divided by TEIP at the start) and a health index (biodiversity integrity and fire impact).

docs.title: Part 3: Water account
docs.text:
1. Converted rainfall and evapotranspiration to volumes per watershed (1 mm = 10 m³/ha), estimated lakes and reservoirs from surface × depth, rivers in river-standard units (length × discharge), and soil and vegetation water as half of actual evapotranspiration.
  2. Computed total inputs (W2), total outputs (W3), the net ecosystem water balance (W4 = W2 − W3), accessible water resources (W6 to W8), total water use (W9, W12) and the use-intensity (W7 / W9), sustainable-use and health indices.

Tools Used

Tool Purpose Google Earth Engine Sentinel-2 processing, SIAC atmospheric correction, spectral indices, building counts Random Forest Tree-cover regression and land cover classification QGIS Mapping, watershed and river layers, overlays, SRTM download plugin SAGA GIS Gaussian smoothing of the landscape indices Google Earth (very-high-resolution imagery) Visual interpretation of validation points

docs.title: Land cover account
docs.text:
• Both maps are reliable: overall accuracy is 91.4 % in 2018 and 93.0 % in 2023, with a Kappa index of 0.9 for both dates.
  • 18 % of the territory changed land cover between 2018 and 2023 (91,157 ha out of 493,045 ha); the remaining 82 % stayed stable.
  • Settlements grew by 421 ha (+39 %), rice paddies by 8 %, cropland by 27 % and sugarcane by 7 %, driven by population growth and internal migration.
  • Closed forest fell by 26 % (−22,404 ha) and semi-open forest by 11 %, mainly through conversion to savanna, bush fires, charcoal making and timber use; overall forest loss is about 11 % in five years (2.2 % per year).
  • Woodland increased by 1,570 ha thanks to village and community reforestation, while raphia palm swamp (−56 ha), gallery forest (−86 ha) and inland water (−13 %) all shrank.

Land cover account: opening stocks, formation (gains), consumption (losses) and closing stocks, in hectares.

Net change by class, 2018–2023. Closed forest lost 22,404 ha, while cropland gained 11,760 ha.

docs.title: Ecosystem infrastructure account
docs.text:
• Potential grew where land is artificialised or farmed (urban +20 %, agriculture +61 %), but fell for forest (−11 %), wetland vegetation (−14 %), savanna (−10 %) and wetlands (−10 %), so the total TEIP across all units is about 6–7 % lower in 2023 than in 2018 (roughly 1 % per year).
  • The park's core zone lost 2.75 % of its landscape potential over five years (0.55 % per year) and the protection zone about 6 %, mainly because forest is turning into savanna after fires.
  • River potential barely changed overall, but the large Amboromalandy dam and the small rice-irrigation dams fragment rivers around Marovoay.
  • The composite ecosystem health index is below 1 (0.88 in 2023), which indicates a degradation of ecosystem health.

TEIP by watershed in 2018 and 2023: the highest values follow the core zone of the park.

Change in TEIP by landscape unit, computed from the values of the infrastructure account.

Landscape fragmentation index by watershed: the south of the study area, outside the park, is the most fragmented.

docs.title: Water account
docs.text:
• Mean annual rainfall dropped from 1,980 mm to 1,674 mm (−15 %) and actual evapotranspiration from 1,533 mm to 1,132 mm (−26 %).
  • The net ecosystem water balance fell by 22 % (about −4.4 % per year), the total renewable water resource by 20 % and the stock of lakes and reservoirs by 8 %, while secondary (irrigation) water rose by 23 %.
  • Total water needs rose from 4.24 to 5.84 billion m³ (+38 %), driven by irrigation (about 25,500 m³ per hectare) and domestic use (about 90 L per household per day), but they stay well below the accessible surplus.
  • The water-use intensity index stays at 1.00, the global sustainable-use index at 0.95 and the water health index at 0.85, so water use shows no depletion risk and water health is stable, although the margin is shrinking.

Mean annual precipitation and actual evapotranspiration by landscape unit, 2018 vs 2023.

Basic ecosystem water account for 2023 (1,000 m³ unless stated otherwise).

Key water account totals: inputs and net balance fall while water needs rise.

docs.title: Limitations and next steps
docs.text:
• Most hydrological inputs are global datasets that I resampled to 1 km; household numbers for 2023 are a proxy based on visible buildings, which can miss houses hidden under dense vegetation.
  • Land cover is mapped at 10 m, so classification quality drives the reliability of every other account.
  • Next steps are to add the carbon account and the total ecosystem capability account, to value the accounts in monetary terms, and to extend them to the whole Boeny region.

docs.title: Automated Detection of Private Vegetable Gardens Using Remote Sensing and Deep Learning, and Structuring of Road Traffic Activity Data
docs.text: Selected samples: RGB image, ground truth, model prediction and correct/error map for Random Forest (left) and ResNet34-UNet (right).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I built a U-Net (ResNet-34 encoder) pipeline that detects and classifies private gardens (allotment gardens, individual vegetable gardens and ornamental gardens) from 20 cm IGN orthophotographs and NDVI / MSAVI2 spectral indices, and I structured an open road-traffic database for France. Both parts support the assessment of how people are exposed to pollutants in soils and air (INERIS, French National Institute for Industrial Environment and Risks).

Study Area: Île-de-France (model training, about 12,000 km²) and a 25 × 25 km area of the Oise department (independent test); road-traffic inventory covering metropolitan France Duration: February 2026 – July 2026 (Master's thesis defended 13 August 2026) Role: Solo project (internship at INERIS, supervised by two engineers) Status: Completed

docs.title: Methods & Tools
docs.text:
Data Sources

  • BD ORTHO® orthophotographs, IGN, 20 cm resolution (Île-de-France for training, Oise 2024 for testing)
  • MOS (Mode d'Occupation des Sols) of Île-de-France, Institut Paris Région: land-use inventory used to build ground-truth garden masks
  • Open road-traffic data (annual average daily traffic, TMJA) published by French departments

docs.title: Part 1: Garden detection
docs.text:
1. Rasterised the MOS garden classes into 20 cm masks aligned with the orthophoto tiles (four classes: non-garden, allotment, individual vegetable and ornamental gardens).
  2. Computed NDVI and MSAVI2, stacked them with the image bands, and cut the data into 512 × 512 px tiles (3,330 tiles, split 70 / 10 / 20 % for training, validation and test).
  3. Normalised and augmented the tiles (Albumentations), then trained a U-Net with an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 encoder (balanced focal loss, early stopping) and a Random Forest baseline.
  4. Evaluated both models with confusion matrices, overall accuracy, Cohen's Kappa and per-class precision, recall, F1 and IoU, then applied the U-Net to an independent area of the Oise.

Methodological workflow, from the 20 cm orthoimages, DHM, BDNB and land-use map to the final land cover map.

docs.title: Part 2: Road-traffic database
docs.text:
1. Wrote Python scripts that query departmental open-data portals and APIs, harmonised the traffic data and loaded it into a PostgreSQL / PostGIS database.

Traffic-data pipeline: from heterogeneous open-data formats to a structured, attribute-documented database keyed by a unique ID.

Tools Used

Tool Purpose Python (rasterio, NumPy, scikit-learn, Albumentations) Raster preprocessing, spectral indices, data augmentation, Random Forest baseline U-Net with ResNet-34 encoder Semantic segmentation of gardens Google Colab (GPU) Model training and inference QGIS Spatial joins and layer merging PostgreSQL / PostGIS Storage and structuring of the road-traffic database

docs.title: Garden detection
docs.text:
• The U-Net reached 83 % overall accuracy (Kappa 0.57) on the Île-de-France test set, against 58 % (Kappa 0.37) for Random Forest.
  • On an independent area of the Oise, the U-Net reached 78 % overall accuracy (Kappa 0.56): allotment gardens were detected best (IoU 82 %, recall 92 %) and individual vegetable gardens reached an IoU of 56 % (recall 81 %, precision 64 %).
  • Individual vegetable gardens remain the hardest class because of their spectral variability and their confusion with other vegetated surfaces; ornamental gardens show many false positives (precision 55 %).

Random Forest baseline: per-class metrics

U-Net (ResNet-34): per-class metrics

The U-Net clearly outperforms the Random Forest on non-garden and allotment gardens, while individual vegetable and ornamental gardens remain difficult for both models.
